blocks.text: 1. Group Normalization

blocks.alt: Channels get grouped together, forming group normalization

blocks.text: Instance Normalization, the previous topic, normalizes each channel entirely separately. Group Normalization sits at a genuinely deliberate middle ground between that approach and Layer Normalization's own broader grouping.
It works by splitting channels into groups, normalizing within each group separately, a genuinely tunable design covered in full depth throughout this topic.
2. The Spectrum Between Layer And Instance Normalization

blocks.alt: Layer norm uses all channels, group norm sits in between, and instance norm uses each channel

blocks.text: This connects back to Layer Normalization and Instance Normalization, both already covered in this module. Layer Normalization treats every channel as one giant group, computing shared statistics across all of them together.

Instance Normalization sits at the opposite extreme, treating each channel as its own separate group entirely; Group Normalization introduces a genuinely tunable number of groups in between these two extremes, covered further in the next section.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Technique","Number of groups"],"rows":[["Layer Normalization, already covered","One giant group containing every channel"],["Instance Normalization, already covered","Every channel is its own separate group"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Why This Gap Genuinely Matters

A genuinely real practical gap exists between the two extremes already covered in the previous section. Related channels often encode meaningfully connected information, such as several channels together representing edges at different orientations.

Neither one giant group, already covered as Layer Normalization's approach, nor every channel fully separate, already covered as Instance Normalization's approach, always captures that connected structure well.
4. The Number Of Groups Hyperparameter

blocks.alt: The number of groups controls the group size

blocks.text: A genuinely important hyperparameter, the number of groups, controls this middle ground directly. This connects back to the number of channels, already covered in Instance Normalization, since channels get divided evenly into that many groups.

Each group's own statistics get computed and normalized entirely separately, a genuinely direct generalization of both Layer Normalization and Instance Normalization, already covered as the two extreme special cases of this same idea.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Setting the number of groups to exactly 1 recovers Layer Normalization exactly, and setting it equal to the total number of channels recovers Instance Normalization exactly, confirming the spectrum already covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 5. Inheriting Batch Independence

blocks.alt: Group normalization has no batch dependence

blocks.text: This connects back to Layer Normalization's own batch independence, already covered in that topic. Group Normalization inherits this same genuinely important property, since its statistics come from within a single example's own channels.

Statistics never depend on other examples in the batch, working correctly even with a batch of exactly 1, exactly the same genuinely valuable property already covered for both Layer Normalization and Instance Normalization.
6. Why Small Batch Sizes Genuinely Matter

blocks.alt: Group norm still works well with a small batch size

blocks.text: This connects back to Batch Normalization's own genuine struggle with small batches, already covered in its own topic. Some Convolutional Neural Network tasks, covered later in this course, genuinely require small batch sizes.

Genuinely large images or memory constraints can force genuinely small batch sizes, a real, practical situation where Batch Normalization's own reliance on large batches, already covered, becomes a genuine liability.
7. The Original Motivation Behind Group Normalization

blocks.alt: Object detection and segmentation often need small batches, motivating group norm

blocks.text: The genuinely original motivation behind Group Normalization traces directly to Object Detection tasks, covered later in this course, where this exact small-batch problem, already covered in the previous section, was especially severe.

Genuinely large images and memory limits often force genuinely small batch sizes there, making Batch Normalization's own approach unreliable while Group Normalization's batch-independent statistics, already covered, remained genuinely stable.
8. The Same Learnable Parameters
This connects back to gamma and beta, already covered across every normalization technique in this module. Group Normalization uses the exact same two learnable parameters, applied per channel.

These let the network genuinely fine-tune each group's normalized output, learned through the same Backpropagation process already familiar from every other weight and every other normalization technique covered in this module.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Group Normalization Is Genuinely The Right Choice

blocks.alt: Computer vision with a small batch points toward using group normalization

blocks.text: Convolutional Neural Network tasks, covered later in this course, with genuinely small batch sizes are a direct case for Group Normalization, since its batch independence, already covered in this topic, directly avoids Batch Normalization's own genuine struggle there.

Wanting genuinely more structure than Instance Normalization's fully separate channels allow is another genuine case, since its tunable group count, already covered, offers a genuinely useful middle ground between the two extremes.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates Group Normalization's core computation, dividing channels into groups and normalizing each group entirely separately.

code.content:
import numpy as np

def group_norm(activations, num_groups, gamma, beta, epsilon=1e-5):
    # activations shape: (batch_size, channels, height, width), already covered as the key idea in this topic
    batch_size, channels, height, width = activations.shape
    grouped = activations.reshape(batch_size, num_groups, channels // num_groups, height, width)

    group_mean = grouped.mean(axis=(2, 3, 4), keepdims=True)
    group_var = grouped.var(axis=(2, 3, 4), keepdims=True)
    normalized = (grouped - group_mean) / np.sqrt(group_var + epsilon)
    normalized = normalized.reshape(batch_size, channels, height, width)

    gamma_r = gamma.reshape(1, -1, 1, 1)
    beta_r = beta.reshape(1, -1, 1, 1)
    return gamma_r * normalized + beta_r  # the same learnable parameters already covered in this topic

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
activations = rng.normal(loc=5.0, scale=2.0, size=(2, 6, 4, 4))  # 2 examples, 6 channels, 4x4 spatial
gamma = np.ones(6)
beta = np.zeros(6)

output = group_norm(activations, num_groups=3, gamma=gamma, beta=beta)  # 6 channels split into 3 groups of 2
print("Output shape (unchanged from input):", output.shape)
print("Group Normalization applied with 3 groups, already covered as the tunable hyperparameter in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example with num_groups set to 1 would reproduce Layer Normalization exactly, and setting it to 6, the total channel count, would reproduce Instance Normalization exactly, confirming the spectrum already covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Group Normalization splits channels into groups, normalizing within each group separately.
It sits on a spectrum between Layer Normalization, one giant group, and Instance Normalization, every channel separate.
The number of groups is a tunable hyperparameter generalizing both of those techniques as special cases.
It inherits batch independence, working correctly even with a batch of exactly 1.
It was originally motivated by Object Detection tasks facing memory-constrained, small batch sizes.
It uses the same learnable gamma and beta parameters already covered throughout this module.
It is especially valuable for small-batch Convolutional Neural Network tasks where Batch Normalization struggles.
It offers more structure than Instance Normalization while remaining fully batch independent.
Next up: Weight Normalization, a technique that normalizes the weights themselves rather than the activations.
